How do you price a stay across nights with different rates?
How does this change for a chain with central inventory and channel partners?
pit: Check-then-insert availability races.
Holds without expiry.
Assigning physical rooms at booking time.

questions.q: LLD: design a thread-safe circuit breaker library (closed, open, half-open states, failure-rate window, probes, events). What makes it correct under concurrency?
questions.a:
### Behaviour
- **Closed**: calls pass; outcomes are recorded in a sliding window (count- or time-based). If the failure rate exceeds a threshold (for example 50% over at least 20 calls), the breaker opens.
- **Open**: calls fail fast with {{BrokenCircuitException}} for a break duration.
- **Half-open**: after the break, allow a limited number of trial calls; if they succeed, close; if any fails, open again.

### Classes
| Class | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| {{CircuitBreakerOptions}} | thresholds, minimum throughput, window, break duration, which exceptions count as failures |
| {{SlidingWindow}} | thread-safe success and failure counts (ring of buckets) |
| {{CircuitBreaker}} | state machine, {{ExecuteAsync(Func<CancellationToken, Task<T>>)}} |
| {{ICircuitBreakerEvents}} | OnOpened, OnHalfOpened, OnClosed for logging and metrics |
| {{TimeProvider}} | injected clock for deterministic tests |

### Concurrency correctness
- State and transition timestamps change via **compare-and-swap** ({{Interlocked.CompareExchange}}) or a short lock; only one thread may perform each transition.
- Half-open must admit **exactly N probes**, not every caller that arrives in the same millisecond: use an atomic permit counter.
- Recording outcomes must not take a global lock per call on hot paths; bucketed counters with Interlocked operations scale.
- Cancellations and timeouts initiated by the caller should not count as dependency failures.

In production, prefer a proven library (Polly v8, Microsoft.Extensions.Resilience); this design explains what those libraries do.
questions.dia:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Closed
  Closed --> Open: failure ratio above threshold with minimum throughput
  Open --> HalfOpen: break duration elapsed
  HalfOpen --> Closed: probe calls succeed
  HalfOpen --> Open: any probe fails
pts: Closed, Open, Half-open with sliding-window failure ratio.
Minimum throughput before opening.
Atomic transitions with CompareExchange.
Exactly N half-open probes via permit counter.
Caller cancellations are not failures; prefer Polly in production.
questions.ex: A home-grown breaker let every waiting request through when it moved to half-open, so 400 calls hit a recovering card processor at once and knocked it over again. Limiting half-open to three atomic probe permits, excluding caller cancellations from failures and testing transitions with FakeTimeProvider made recovery smooth; the team later replaced it with Polly v8 and kept the tests as a specification.
fu: Count-based or time-based windows: when each?
How do you share breaker state across instances, and should you?
What metrics should the breaker emit?
pit: Letting all callers through in half-open.
Counting client cancellations as dependency failures.
A global lock on every call.

questions.q: LLD: design an embedded key-value store (put, get, delete, range scans) that survives crashes. Explain the write-ahead log, memtable, SSTables, compaction and the class design.
questions.a:
### Write path
1. Append the operation to the **write-ahead log (WAL)** and flush (fsync) according to the durability setting.
2. Apply it to the **memtable**: an in-memory sorted structure (skip list or balanced tree).
3. When the memtable reaches a size limit, freeze it and write it to disk as an immutable, sorted **SSTable** file with an index and a Bloom filter; then the WAL segment can be deleted.

### Read path
Check the memtable, then the frozen memtable, then SSTables from newest to oldest. Bloom filters skip files that cannot contain the key; the per-file index finds the block. Deletes are **tombstones** that hide older values until compaction removes them.

### Compaction
Merge SSTables to remove overwritten values and tombstones and to keep the number of files small: **size-tiered** (good write throughput, more space amplification) or **levelled** (better read and space amplification, more write amplification).

### Crash recovery
On start, load the SSTable manifest, then replay WAL segments newer than the last flushed memtable. A checksum per WAL record detects torn writes; recovery stops at the first corrupt record.

### Classes
| Class | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| {{Store}} | public API, single-writer lock, read snapshots |
| {{WriteAheadLog}} | append, fsync policy, segment rotation, replay |
| {{MemTable}} | sorted map with size tracking |
| {{SsTableWriter}} / {{SsTableReader}} | blocks, index, Bloom filter, checksums |
| {{Manifest}} | which files exist at which level; updated atomically (write new, rename) |
| {{Compactor}} | background merges, throttled |
questions.dia:
flowchart LR
  W[Put or Delete] --> WAL[Append to WAL and fsync]
  WAL --> MT[Memtable: sorted in memory]
  MT -->|full| IMM[Frozen memtable]
  IMM -->|flush| L0[Level 0 SSTables]
  L0 -->|compaction| L1[Level 1 SSTables]
  R[Get] --> MT
  R --> IMM
  R -->|Bloom filter, then index| L0
  R --> L1
pts: WAL first, then memtable; flush to immutable SSTables.
Reads: memtable, frozen memtable, SSTables newest first, Bloom filters.
Tombstones for deletes; compaction removes them.
Size-tiered vs levelled compaction trade-offs.
Recovery: manifest plus WAL replay with checksums.
questions.ex: An audit-event buffer stored events in an append-only file and rewrote the whole file to apply deletes, so restarts took 20 minutes. Rebuilding it on an LSM design (WAL, memtable, SSTables with Bloom filters, levelled compaction) made writes constant time, restarts replay only the latest WAL segment in seconds, and range scans by time stay ordered.
fu: What is write amplification and how does compaction affect it?
How would you add snapshot reads?
What fsync policy would you choose and why?
pit: Acknowledging writes before the WAL is durable.
Non-atomic manifest updates.
Unthrottled compaction stalling foreground writes.

cheat:
### Method
Requirements -> entities and responsibilities -> relationships + interfaces at variation points -> class + sequence diagrams -> state machine + concurrency -> code the hard part -> extensibility, tests, trade-offs.

### Modelling rules
Behaviour lives with the data · value objects for money, ids, quantities · state machines for lifecycles · composition over inheritance (inherit only true subtypes like chess pieces) · reference other aggregates by id · result types for business outcomes · inject TimeProvider and I/O ports.

### Concurrency toolkit
CAS (Interlocked) for single fields · lock per aggregate, consistent lock order for many · holds with expiry · idempotency keys · single-writer partitions for high throughput · DB conditional updates / row versions when persisted · stress tests asserting invariants.

### Classic LLD problems
Parking lot (size as data, atomic spot claim) · vending machine (State) · elevator (LOOK + dispatcher strategy) · library (Book vs BookCopy) · Splitwise (minor units, greedy settle-up) · ATM (authorise, dispense, confirm/reverse) · LRU/TTL cache · rate limiter · pub/sub bus · bank account (policies, lock order) · order book (price levels, FIFO) · booking (all-or-nothing holds) · inventory (OnHand - Reserved) · coupons (atomic redemption) · rule engine (expression tree, versioned) · approvals (four-eyes, subject hash) · ledger (zero-sum journals, reversals) · audit log (same transaction, hash chain).

### Say this
"Size is data, not a subclass." "The invariant lives in the aggregate." "Holds expire." "Unknown outcomes are a state." "Here is what I am not building, and the trigger to add it."

### Added class diagrams to remember
- Logger: logger buffers into a channel, fans out batches to sink interfaces, formatters per sink.
- Splitwise: group owns expenses, each expense has a split strategy, a planner minimises settlement transfers.
- Cache: dictionary plus linked list, eviction policy interface, injected clock for TTL tests.
- Cart: pricing engine runs an ordered list of pricing rules.
- Chess: abstract piece generates candidate moves; a validator applies check and special rules.
- Approval workflow: states plus guarded transitions; maker cannot be checker.
